items.title: EJF Capital to Build BTR Community in Indianapolis
items.description: EJF Capital to Build BTR Community in Indianapolis EJF Capital LP, a global alternative asset management firm, announced that it has closed a joint venture with Onyx+East, a homebuilder based in Indianapolis, to develop Monon 21, a 57-unit build-to-rent community in Indianapolis, Indiana. The project will consist of 53 townhomes across 12 three-story buildings and four single-family homes. Construction financing was provided by Stock Yards Bank & Trust Company. Located in a Qualified Opportunity Zone, the development will transform a former industrial property into a residential community. With demolition complete and site preparation underway, leasing is expected to begin in early 2028, with construction completion anticipated in early 2029. The joint venture brings together Onyx+East’s experience developing residential communities throughout Indianapolis with EJF’s expertise in opportunity zone investments. Each rental home at Monon 21 will feature three bedrooms, two-and-a-half bathrooms, and a private attached garage. Monon 21 is EJF’s 26th investment in multifamily and commercial developments since 2018. Join us for the Connect Midwest Multifamily conference on the afternoon of Tuesday, June 8, 2027, at Joe’s Live in Rosemont, Illinois. Connect Inside The Story EJF Capital About Jasmine Kilman Jasmine Kilman is Content Director of Connect Commercial Real Estate, covering Chicago and greater Chicagoland, the Midwest, Seattle, and the Pacific Northwest. She covers industry trends, transaction deals, market research, and produces daily news stories. With experience in marketing and communications for academic nonprofits and corporate clients, including Hearst Media, Hilton, and Coldwell Banker, Kilman has written about commercial real estate, environmental, social, and corporate governance (ESG), technology, healthcare, and philanthropy. She was born and raised in California and graduated with a degree in public relations. In her spare time, Kilman enjoys hiking and traveling to new locations with her family. items.title: Promise Robotics raises $25M to scale automated homebuilding
items.description: Any way you look at it, homebuilding comes down to three things: how many homes a company can produce and sell, how much it costs to produce them, and how consistently the business can turn those homes into positive net margins. There’s no getting around throughput. Homebuilding leaders who do those three things well rarely have qualms about finding ways to do them even better. Innovation, however, is another matter. Homebuilders like innovation. Many believe it's necessary, even inevitable. But do they have to embrace it? Do they have to change how they operate to adopt and integrate it? Do they dare risk what works, warts and all, for what hasn’t yet proven to solve the throughput riddle economically? Evidence suggests that if innovation were a necessity rather than a choice, or a known rather than a leap into a chasm of unknowns, more of the dozens of companies launched over the past decade with promises to transform homebuilding, lower costs and make homes more attainable would still be in business today. Which brings us to Promise Robotics , a company whose name might as well be its business plan: Say what you're going to do, and then do what you say. Fresh off a multiyear commercial agreement with D.R. Horton , the nation's largest homebuilder, Promise Robotics today announced a $25 million Series B financing round led by White Star Capital , with participation from Horizons Ventures , Radical Ventur es and the Public Sector Pension Investment Board . The financing follows Promise's agreement to support the production of more than 1,250 homes for D.R. Horton as the company prepares to bring its first U.S. manufacturing facility online in Phoenix in 2027. Promise already operates production facilities in Calgary and Nisku, Alberta, and reports more than 2,000 housing units under contract across three markets. For Promise co-founder and CEO Ramtin Attar, the latest investment adrenaline shot is an opportunity to show that the company has figured out how to turn advanced robotics, artificial intelligence and factory-built construction into a sustainable business capable of weathering homebuilding's inevitable ups and downs, which, by the way, are now mostly downs. That's where this homebuilding innovation’s never-ending story takes a turn. Because the history of industrialized homebuilding is littered with companies that developed impressive technologies, attracted enthusiastic investors, and secured commitments from builders, only to discover that the economics of operating their businesses – and the critical factor of the time value of money in a stubbornly high cost of money backdrop – were far less forgiving than the promise of their innovations. Attar is all too familiar with that history. So are his investors. "Every investor's question often starts by asking what went wrong with Katerra, what went wrong with X and Y and Z," Attar told HousingWire TBD in an exclusive interview. His determination is to transform Promise Robotics into a fundamentally different kind of construction technology business, one that uses venture capital to develop its technology platform while seeking lower-cost financing to scale its physical production capacity. "We have been very clear about what we want to use this funding for," Attar said. "It's not for funding factories; it's for funding the platform." Attar’s laser clarity on how the strategy will be operationalized may prove more important to Promise's long-term prospects than the robots themselves. The distinction goes directly to the problem that has defeated so many would-be homebuilding innovators: scaling manufacturing capacity without accumulating fixed costs that become unsustainable when housing demand weakens. A smaller factory, and a different cost structure One of the more revealing details from Attar's latest interview concerns what Promise calls a factory. The company's Phoenix operation is being set up in a 16,000-square-foot warehouse with existing electrical infrastructure and a loading bay. Attar said the facility requires almost no tenant improvements and is under a relatively short-term lease. Importantly, the robotic equipment itself can be ported from market to market. "It was the same two robots that were producing homes in Calgary," Attar said. "We just moved them to Phoenix two weeks ago. They're already set up. We're just hiring, and we're going to start producing." Portability is central to Promise's effort to avoid the fixed-cost exposure associated with large, purpose-built manufacturing facilities. The company can theoretically deploy equipment in markets where customer demand supports production, rather than making a substantial permanent investment in each market before securing sufficient orders. The model still depends on reliable demand, efficient material handling, trained workers, and economical installation. But it offers more flexibility to respond to changing market conditions. Attar also described an operational improvement that provides a clearer view of the company's economic progress. When Promise initially relied on outside contractors to install its prefabricated components, installation costs averaged about C$9 per square foot. After developing its own installation workforce, the company reduced that figure to about C$4.50. That 50% reduction is significant, though it applies to installation costs rather than to total home construction costs. For Attar, it shows that the opportunity to improve construction economics extends beyond robotic manufacturing. "There are still tremendous gains to be made on the human side of things," he said. The company's recursive learning process increasingly involves understanding labor requirements, installation sequencing, material logistics and how production crews work alongside existing trades. items.title: Austin Office Campus Lands $228M Refinancing Deal
items.description: Developer Jay Paul Co. has secured $227.5M in green financing to recapitalize an 881K SF office campus in Austin. The deal marks the largest commercial property assessed clean energy, or C-PACE , transaction in Texas to date, according to Nuveen Green Capital, which closed the financing for the property. Unsplash/micheile henderson The $227.5M refinanced a construction loan on Springdale Green, a Class-A office campus at 1011 Springdale Road, Nuveen announced in a press release . C-PACE allows commercial property owners to secure long-term, low-cost financing for sustainable projects. The fixed-rate loans are often used for properties looking to make upgrades in terms of energy efficiency, water conservation and renewable energy. "The closing on Springdale Green reinforces the widespread adoption of C-PACE by institutional owners and developers," Cory Jubran, senior director of originations at Nuveen, said in an emailed statement. "C-PACE’s flexibility and lower cost of capital compared to other forms of finance are helping drive large-scale development, including notable projects like this one in Austin, across Texas, and in other MSAs." C-PACE momentum has picked up over the past couple of years, with a record $3.7B deployed in 2025, a 53% year-over-year surge, according to nonprofit PACENation. Springdale Green is a LEED Gold and Fitwel-certified property. It comprises two six-story office buildings on a 30-acre site and features a fitness center, a covered parking garage and more than 31K SF of outdoor space. Austin's office market posted strong net absorption in the third quarter, reaching 124K SF in Class-A space and 253K SF total, according to a CBRE report . That total surpassed the 50K SF posted in the second quarter as tenants took substantially more space than they vacated. Average office asking rents trended "gradually higher" throughout the quarter, with Class-A office space averaging $58.54 per SF, a 2.5% year-over-year increase, according to the report. items.title: Westcore Entity Pays $51.1M for Seattle-Area Light Industrial Campus
items.description: Westcore Entity Pays $51.1M for Seattle-Area Light Industrial Campus A Westcore-affiliated entity acquired Woodinville Corporate Center I, a multi-tenant, light industrial park located in the Woodinville submarket east of Seattle, in a transaction reported to be worth $51.1 million. Located at 17606–17683 128th Place NE, along the SR-522 Corridor, Woodinville Corporate Center I was sold by Blackstone's Link Logistics, one of the largest owners and operators of last-mile warehouse and industrial real estate in North America. Woodinville Corporate Center I contains four buildings totaling roughly 172,000 square feet. Completed in 1988 and 1989, the concrete tilt-up buildings offer clear heights of 16 to 24 feet, 45 dock-high doors, 29 drive-in doors and 227 parking stalls, with suites ranging from approximately 8,300 to 33,300 square feet. The property is 100% leased to nine tenants. The buildings are part of the 890,000 square foot, multi-phase Woodinville Corporate Center industrial complex constructed between 1979 and 1991. Woodinville Corporate Center’s Phases II, III & IV were acquired by Terrano Realty in 2025 for around $232 million. That purchase consisted of nine buildings containing 720,000 square feet across 43 acres. Connect Inside The Story About Allen Wolfsheimer Allen Wolfsheimer is Content Director at Connect CRE. items.title: HSBC Sells $300M Of Data Center Debt Tied To Stargate Project At Big Discount
items.description: Financial giant HSBC has sold $300M in data center construction debt at less than 90 cents on the dollar, the latest sign of lender wariness of the growing risks facing large-scale data center development. Wikimedia Commons/Barry Caruth The debt is part of an $18B financing package assembled by 20 banks for Project Jupiter, a massive data center development in Doña Ana County, New Mexico, Bloomberg reports . The construction financing closed last year after being marketed to lenders under the code name Project Miner amid a boom in debt financing for hyperscalers ’ artificial intelligence campuses. But Project Jupiter has since run into problems. The 1,400-acre campus is being developed by Blue Owl-backed Stack Infrastructure for OpenAI , Oracle and SoftBank 's Stargate initiative and could eventually reach 2.45 gigawatts. The project has faced concerns about potential delays due to community opposition and regulatory hurdles involving air and pipeline permits. In September, Oracle sent the developers a force majeure notice that would allow it to defer payments if the project is delayed or derailed. HSBC reportedly unloaded the $300M chunk of its debt tied to the project immediately after the force majeure notice, according to Bloomberg. HSBC isn't the only lender that has tried to reduce its exposure to Project Jupiter. Dutch bank ING is also reportedly seeking buyers for $25M of debt backing the development, along with nearly a dozen other data center loans. The debt sales are just the latest sign of growing volatility across data center credit markets. Lenders are showing concerns about escalating risks surrounding data center development — from community opposition and restrictive regulations to uncertainty about the future of AI cloud providers and alarm at the pace of hyperscale infrastructure spending. Jensen Huang ’s sudden resignation from Nvidia has only added to the unease surrounding the sector. Lender anxiety has been most apparent in the structured debt markets. In recent weeks, yields on some bonds tied to data center projects have climbed into the double digits, while even debt issued by major hyperscalers has traded at higher spreads than the investment-grade standard. At the same time, credit default swaps on data center debt have hit an all-time high. Analysts also say the lenders are concerned about concentration risk . The scale of capital required for the AI data center boom is unprecedented, and there is only so much capital that any lender is comfortable having tied up in just a handful of companies all pursuing broadly similar strategies. items.description: Zillow: CPI Shelter Forecast, November 2026 Zillow forecasts 3.0% rent inflation, 3.6% OER inflation annually in October, as measured by the Consumer Price Index. Written by Treh Manhertz on November 17, 2026 New shelter inflation numbers from the Bureau of Labor Statistics are scheduled to be released on Thursday, December 10, 2026 at 8:30 ET. Key Takeaway CPI housing inflation is expected to firm into the end of the year. We currently forecast annual rent inflation to finish 2026 around 3.0% and OER near 3.5%. Part of the year-end rise is mechanical, as the BLS folded October 2025's increase ,missed during the government shutdown, into April 2026. This adjustment will add about 0.3 points to the true underlying annual rate until April 2027. From last month's forecast, the year-end outlook was revised up for OER (3.44% to 3.53%) and down for rent (3.06% to 3.04%). New-lease rents have been growing at their fastest pace of 2025-2026, no longer pulling down housing inflation measures. Forecasts for on-market rents have been revised higher for the past few months. items.title: A Better Credit Score Could Save Buyers $864 a Year on a Typical Mortgage
items.description: A Better Credit Score Could Save Buyers $864 a Year on a Typical Mortgage New Zillow analysis finds that in October 2026, buyers in the highest credit band got a mortgage rate 36 basis points lower than buyers in the lowest band Written by Kara Ng on November 17, 2026 Key findings In October 2026, buyers with a credit score of 740 or higher were quoted a 7.23% rate on average on a 30-year fixed mortgage. Those with a credit score between 680 and 739 typically were quoted a 7.45% rate, while those with a score below 680 on average were quoted a rate of 7.59%, a 36-basis-point spread between the highest and lowest credit bands. With a 20% down payment, the total monthly payment on a typical U.S. home in October, worth $364,812, would have been $2,656 in the lowest credit score band and $2,584 in the highest. That’s an annual savings of $864 for those with the best credit scores. As of October 2026, a median-income household with a score of 740 or higher could afford a $317,572 home, versus $308,924 for a score below 680. That gap puts about 21,500 more active listings within reach nationwide. A higher credit score can be worth real money. A buyer with a strong credit score (740 or higher) can save more than $800 per year compared to a buyer with a low credit score (300-679) when buying the typical U.S. home. Those savings would have brought about 21,500 additional listings within budget nationwide for a median-income household in October. A better credit score changes the affordability math Home buyers with higher credit scores often receive a lower mortgage rate on their loan, which means a lower monthly payment. In October, the average mortgage rate offered to buyers with strong credit scores was 7.23%, while buyers with low credit scores were quoted a 7.59% rate, on average. For a typical U.S. home ($364,812) with a 20% down payment, that would mean a difference of $72 in each month’s mortgage payment, or $864 a year. Buyers with good scores of 680 to 739 sat in between, with a 7.45% rate, on average. That means they would pay $348 a year less than someone with a low credit score, but $516 a year more than someone with a strong credit score. These savings stretch a home buyer's budget, bringing more homes within reach. In October, a median-income household with a low credit score could afford a $308,924 home — meaning it would spend no more than 30% of its income on housing costs — given the average mortgage rate on offer. If that same median-income household had a strong credit score, it could afford a $317,572 home, an increase of about $8,650 in buying power. Where a better score is worth the most A better credit score brings the biggest potential savings in coastal markets, where home values are higher. Across the 50 largest metro areas, moving from a low credit score to a strong one saves anywhere from $45 a month in Pittsburgh to $304 in San Jose. A home buyer in San Jose could save $3,648 a year by moving from a low credit score to a strong one, followed by San Francisco ($2,688), Los Angeles ($2,256), San Diego ($2,208) and New York ($1,740). San Jose buyers would also enjoy the largest gain in buying power from improving their credit score at $18,778, ahead of Seattle ($14,896), San Francisco ($14,602), Raleigh ($13,688) and Washington, D.C. ($13,489). The smallest annual savings are in Pittsburgh ($540), Oklahoma City ($576), Memphis ($576) and Cleveland ($588). These are markets where mortgage payments are relatively inexpensive already, so there is less room for improvement with a lower rate. October's rate gap was the narrowest of 2026 The 36-basis-point spread in mortgage rates offered to buyers with strong and low credit scores in October was the narrowest of the year. Across the first 10 months of 2026, the rate difference between the lowest and highest credit bands ranged from 36 basis points in October to 58 basis points in April, with a median of 46 basis points. The monthly payment gap ranged from $72 in October to $110 in April, with a median of about $88, so the typical buyer in the lowest band paid roughly $1,050 a year more than a buyer in the highest band over that stretch. Improving their credit score is not the only way a buyer can secure a better rate. Buyers can also compare offers from multiple lenders , yet few actually do. Among buyers who contacted a lender, 62% contacted only one, according to Zillow's 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report . Methodology Rates come from Zillow's Custom Quotes marketplace and reflect 30-year fixed conventional conforming purchase loans with 20% down or more. Credit bands are 300-679, 680-739 and 740+, and rates are quoted nationally. Quotes do not come from Zillow Home Loans. Data is as of October 2026. items.description: New-Construction Insights: Builders Hold Steady on Price, but Offer Savings via Reduced Rates By Joel Berner Nov 17, 2026 Home Construction Highlights The median listing price for a new home in the United States has barely budged in the last three years, but existing home prices have been falling. Builders have slowed down new construction activity, and the number of new homes for sale this quarter is basically unchanged from last year. Existing home inventory is growing slowly, but faster than new homes. The average new construction buyer pays $258 per month less on interest in the first year of homeownership than the median existing home buyer due to reduced mortgage rates, assuming a $400,000 home purchase with 10% down. For reduced rates fixed through the 30-year life of the loan, new home buyers pay $117 per month less. National Overview The median listing price for newly built homes in the United States rose slightly in the third quarter of 2026, reaching $451,071. This is right in line with where new home prices were last year in the third quarter as well as in the third quarter of 2024. New home listing prices have been remarkably stable throughout the post-pandemic period of elevated mortgage rates. Existing home prices, on the other hand, continued to grow through 2025 but have given up ground so far in 2026. For the third quarter this year, existing home prices came in 1.5% below 2025 levels, landing at $402,883. Builders were quicker to adjust to the realities of muted buyer demand in this high rate environment, while existing home sellers had pricing expectations based on the market from 2021 and 2022 that were slower to dissolve. The overall price softness we’ve seen through 2026 is driven primarily by the existing home segment. The recovery in the number of homes for sale has slowed significantly in 2026 for both new construction and resale homes, as inventory on the market is inching closer to pre-pandemic levels. In 2026Q3, new home inventory grew just 0.1% year over year and existing home inventory grew 3.1%. Existing home sellers have been reluctant to put their homes on the market as selling conditions have softened: falling prices, longer times on market, more price reductions. Builders are facing challenges as well–increased labor and material costs, decreased buyer demand–that have led to the completion rate of new single family homes falling 11.0% year over year in September. New resale listings and newly completed homes are slowly trickling onto the market rather than surging like they were a few years ago. One notable result from the past three quarters of this data series is that builders were cutting listing prices at a higher rate than existing home sellers. We chalked this up to the resale market finally adjusting its expectations and setting initial prices lower, lessening the need for price adjustments, but this quarter existing home price reductions came roaring back. Resellers are now cutting prices on 21.6% of homes for sale while builders are doing the same for 20.9%. Both measures are higher than they were last year at this time, but while builders are steadily increasing their share of price reductions, resale homes with price cuts are resurgent after taking a step back early this year. Regardless of their relative positions, the growing incidence of price reductions for new and existing homes is an indication of softness in the housing market in general and gives reason to expect that the diminished pace of inventory growth will continue. Though there is nearly a $50,000 gap between the median new home price and the median existing home price, new homes tend to be larger (a median of 2,056 square feet compared to 1,790 square feet this quarter). Adjusting for size, this price gap disappears. The median price per square foot for new homes was $218 in 2026Q3 and for existing homes it was $219. This counterintuitive result can be attributed to the three most important factors in real estate: location, location, location. New builds are heavily concentrated in the South and in the suburbs where land is less expensive. If the current trends in listing prices continue, though, we could see the median existing home price per square foot drop back below the same measure for new homes in the coming quarters. The recent pullback by builders is making new construction less impactful in the market than it has been in the past. The new construction share of listings fell from 17.2% in 2025Q3 to 16.7% in 2026Q3 and the new construction premium (the percent difference in median listing price between new and existing homes) rose from 10.3% to 12.0%. Buyers are finding fewer new homes for sale and the ones they do find are relatively more expensive. In September, the median sales price for new homes , which has been falling faster over the past few years than new home asking prices, was $400,400 while for existing homes it was $417,500. This does not imply that a new build in the same neighborhood with similar specifications to an older home is selling at a lower price. It has much more to do with geographic mix. The pricier Northeast, home to some of the hottest home sales markets in the country right now and home to relatively little new construction activity, makes up 11.8% of existing home sales and just 4.7% of new home sales. The more affordable South, where many markets are seeing home sales fall and where new construction activity is heavily concentrated, makes up 61.1% of new home sales to just 46.6% of existing home sales. items.title: A conflict of interest
items.description: Non-QM loans are part of the equation helping investors expand their footprint in the property market. Financing edge: Five-year, interest-only loans can maximize rental margins over short hold periods. Market shift: As institutional investment retreats, mom-and-pop buyers stepped in, acquiring 20% more homes than they sold. Buyer fallout: Heavy investor demand keeps prices and rents high, contributing to locking gig and freelance workers out of ownership. Millions of Americans now embrace freelancing, small-business ownership, or gig-economy careers, but the industry hasn’t widely adopted lending structures that correspond to this shift. Add to that dynamic the increasingly unaffordable price tag for homes, and many would-be homeowners are stuck as renters. Many are renting from similarly minded entrepreneurs: mom-and-pop investors. The difference is that investors are turning to non-QM mortgages to finance property transactions, according to Cotatlity data. Many are doing so to take advantage of interest-only payments. The five-year flip The U.S. housing market offers an ideal proposition to small investors. Rents have increased 25% in the last five years, the federal government has curbed institutional investment, and home equity continues to rise. Investors are responding by reasserting their presence in markets across the U.S. Cotality data shows that the share of investors making home purchases has climbed since mid-2022 and now represents about a third of all transactions. Small investors represent about half of that transaction volume. Investment transactions occur frequently, making them an ideal candidate for interest-only loans. Nearly half of investor hold onto a property for five years or less — that precise timeframe makes an interest-only mortgage worth the equity tradeoff. Most interest-only loans have an initial period of five years before principal repayment begins where monthly commitments are reduced to create wider profit margins on rents. While investors who finance this way won’t reap the benefits of accrued equity, they can profit from the persistently high home prices and a tight inventory that makes short-term commitments profitable. How long does each investor type hold property Data source: Cotality, 2026 The U.S. is short 4.7 million homes . The ones that are available are in high demand. Add in mortgage rates near 7%, and affordability is being tested at its limits. Home prices reflect that squeeze. That dynamic has allowed investors in states like California, where they buy over a third of all homes, to profit on investments financed by interest-only loans. Investors nearly doubled the number of purchases they made in Los Angeles between Q1 and Q2 2026. Home prices jumped 2% during that period. This localized surge in investment is colliding directly with broader national price pressures—a dynamic we analyzed in our piece, Bend It Like Buyers. In major metros, that friction has created a stalemate between buyers and sellers, leaving the door open to more financially flexible investors. Many blame Wall Street. Institutional investors ban themselves Injecting corporate-backed demand into a market where local buyers are already stretched, extends even the most flexible buyers past their breaking point. Local residents who are priced out of home purchases find themselves competing with incoming industrial contractors for the exact same rental inventory. The resulting rent escalation drives up investor yields in the short term, but it simultaneously compresses local household purchasing power and accelerates affordability risk. That has a direct influence on local markets. In states like California, Texas, and Georgia, where investors buy over a third of all homes, prices have risen disproportionately. In Texas, home prices jumped 38% as investor share climbed to 31% between 2020 and 2023. In Georgia, prices jumped 54% alongside an investor share increase to 29%. But the passage of the 21 st Century ROAD to Housing Bill disrupted that playbook. Even before the passage of the bill, Cotality data shows that institutional investment contracted from around 250 home purchases a week to 100. Mom-and-pop investors filled the gap. Small-time landlords entered a market where equity was on the rise, which allowed them to build a cash cushion to insulate them from current high-interest rates and create wider profit margins that allow them to redeploy capital elsewhere. When that equity cushion is layered atop monthly rental income profit, these landlords can offset systemic hurdles such as interest rates and rising home insurance costs. Much of that extra capital is going into increasing their market share. Small mom-and-pop investors purchased 20% more homes than they offloaded last year, according to Cotality data. Their persistent presence is reshaping the housing market. Main street moves in Across the country, investors are the ones with the financial wherewithal to purchase homes in the current high-cost, high-rate environment. This is contributing to keeping costs — from home prices to rents — elevated and widening the gap for aspiring homeowners. Some renters will be blocked from homeowership by these costs. Others will bend and stretch to make the homeownership math work. Some will look to non-QM mortgages themselves. Forward-looking lenders who are optimizing for long-term growth will cater to both sides. There is now a path forward. It may be unconventional, but it is a door through which an increasing number of investors and homeowners are stepping to make the dream of homeownership a reality. items.title: This Week Brings a Chance for Clarity After Mortgage Rates Rise on Hot Inflation and Hawkish Fed Remarks
items.description: This Week Brings a Chance for Clarity After Mortgage Rates Rise on Hot Inflation and Hawkish Fed Remarks Published on November 17th, 2026 by Chen Zhao In A Nutshell: Rates climbed last week following surprising commentary from the Fed potentially hinting at more hikes to come, but there are plenty of opportunities for Fed speakers to clarify their views this week. Last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of big news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target. Notably, a few hours before CPI, Fed Governor Christopher Waller came out with some surprising remarks, putting a 50 bps December hike on the table as a possibility if inflation came in high, which it did. Before he spoke, markets would have assumed an inflation report like the one we got would lead to a guaranteed 25 bps hike. Now markets are assuming the 25 bps hike happens and pricing in some possibility for a larger hike. Subsequent remarks from other Fed officials backed off the 50 bps hike but showed possible support for another hike in January. Previously, markets had assumed that the next hike would happen in March. The net effect of all of this is that markets are now pricing in almost two additional rate hikes by mid-2027 than they were previously, which is why mortgage rates increased last week. The Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy. Finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand. Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much. Investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are New York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow. items.title: Builder Sentiment Continues to Fall on Affordability Concerns
items.description: Builder Sentiment Continues to Fall on Affordability Concerns November 17, 2026 Robert Dietz No Comments Builder confidence has dropped to a 14-year low, dragged down by high mortgage rates, ongoing inflation pressure, elevated energy and material costs, rising labor shortages and hesitant buyers. Builder confidence in the market for newly built single-family homes fell four points to 25 in November, according to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB)/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI). The reading was the lowest since April 2012. The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges, including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability. Stepped up immigration enforcement is affecting labor availability in some markets. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates. Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back. Consequently, single-family home builders are pulling back on construction volumes. In November, 46% of builders reduced prices, the highest share in the post-Covid period, according to the latest HMI survey. The average price reduction held at 6% for an eighth straight month. Meanwhile, 68% of builders offered sales incentives, also a post-Covid high, marking the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders used them. Derived from a monthly survey that NAHB has been conducting for more than 40 years, the NAHB/Wells Fargo HMI gauges builder perceptions of current single-family home sales and sales expectations for the next six months as “good,” “fair” or “poor.” The survey also asks builders to rate traffic of prospective buyers as “high to very high,” “average” or “low to very low.” Scores for each component are then used to calculate a seasonally adjusted index where any number over 50 indicates that more builders view conditions as good than poor. All three of the major HMI indices posted losses in November. The index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, the index gauging future sales expectations dropped two points to 30 and the index charting prospective buyer traffic fell two points to 16 – its lowest level in 15 years, excluding the start of the pandemic in 2020. Looking at the three-month moving averages for regional HMI scores, the Northeast dropped four points to 34, the Midwest fell five points to 35, the South fell three points to 27 and the West posted a three-point decline to 23. The HMI tables can be found at nahb.org/hmi . items.description: An Aspen estate owned by an Australian billionaire for more than a decade has traded hands as the exclusive Colorado resort town’s housing market cools. Former casino and resorts executive James Packer sold the mansion at 1518 West Buttermilk Road for $42.7 million, the Wall Street Journal reported . The price amounts to $2,847 per square foot. The 2-acre property hit the market five months ago with an asking price of $48.9 million. Packer and his ex-wife Erica Packer bought the home in 2013 for $15.6 million. The former couple is parting with the property largely because Erica and their children now live in the U.K. The buyers are tech entrepreneur Alex Davis and his wife, Lindsay Davis, according to property records. Alex Davis is the grandson of late billionaire Marvin Davis, who was an oil magnate that went on to buy Twentieth Century Fox in the early 1980s. Alex founded Dallas-based venture capital firm Disruptive. Christie’s International Real Estate’s Stephanie Lewis and Wendy Wogan held the listing. Compass’ Steven Shane represented the buyers. The 15,000-square-foot home was built in 2006 and has seven bedrooms and seven bathrooms, per the listing with Christie’s. The estate features panoramic views of the mountains. SIGN UP Aspen saw a handful of big-ticket sales this year, but the market is beginning to cool, as year-to-date sales in Aspen and Snowmass were down in dollar volume by 19 percent in October compared to the same period last year, according to Aspen Snowmass Sotheby’s International Realty’s Tim Estin. The top of the luxury market is still in good shape, Lewis said. “While we’ve seen some softening in lower price ranges, demand for truly exceptional properties remains strong,” Lewis said. items.title: Bleak house: Builder confidence hits 14-year low in November
items.description: Bleak house: Builder confidence hits 14-year low in November by John Yellig November 17, 2026 Builder confidence fell to a 14-year low in November, thanks to "high mortgage rates, ongoing inflation pressure, elevated energy and material costs, rising labor shortages and hesitant buyers ," according to the latest survey from the National Association of Home Builders . Specifically, confidence in the single-family home market fell four points to 25 — the lowest since April 2012. Any reading over 50 indicates more builders view conditions as good than poor. “Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today’s economy,” said NAHB Chairman Bill Owens, a homebuilder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio. “Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction.” Regionally, the three-month average for the Northeast dropped four points to 34, the Midwest fell five points to 35, the South fell three points to 27, and the West fell three points to 23. The other three components of the Housing Market Index fell in November as well: The index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, the index gauging future sales expectations dropped two points to 30, and the index charting prospective buyer traffic fell two points to 16 — its lowest level in 15 years besides the beginning of the pandemic in 2020. “The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges, including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability,” NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz said. “Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back.” Read More Related to This Post Ashton Woods names Nicholas Czar SVP of sales HAR named among defendants in new Compass litigation Existing-home sales miss estimates in October Why insurance and property taxes are becoming Houston’s biggest housing obstacles New, pending, closed listings remain depressed in Houston Houston single-family home sales dip 15% in October Home trends you’ll see in 2027, according to Zillow NAR recommends new MLS policy changes amid Compass private-listings kerfuffle Join the conversation Cancel reply Save my name, email, and website in this browser for the next time I comment.

items.title: Dallas Asks Judge to Dismiss City Hall Lawsuit
items.description: Live Poll A little more than three months after a group aiming to force the city to preserve Dallas City Hall filed suit, the city has filed a motion to dismiss it. The Save Dallas City Hall Coalition sued the city in August, alleging that Dallas City Hall’s state of disrepair was tantamount to “demolition by neglect” and is a way for city officials to finagle the eventual tear down of the not even 50-year-old Brutalist building designed by the late I.M. Pei. The suit named the city, Mayor Eric Johnson, all 14 City Council members, as well as City Manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert, Historic Preservation Officer Marcus Watson, and Chief of Real Estate John Johnson. In its motion, the city says that the Coalition hasn’t been personally harmed and lacks standing to sue. It also says that the issues with City Hall’s maintenance began long before the controversial plan to potentially demolish City Hall to pave way for development downtown, and claims of demolition by neglect are inappropriate. “Decisions about repairs to City Hall are intrinsically discretionary, are well within the authority of the city officials making them, and pertain to the balancing of priorities associated with the City’s finite budget,” the motion says. “Additionally, Plaintiff’s assertions of demolition by neglect, abusing City Hall equipment, and breaching fiduciary duties lack a basis in law or fact.” Even prior to the debate over whether City Hall operations should move to another building to make way for developing the site at 1500 Marilla, the deferred maintenance issues at the building were becoming more well known. In August 2025 , D Magazine reported that in a City Council briefing, John Johnson told the Council that he didn’t know how much it would take to get all 500 city buildings properly maintained. “Johnson explained that it is industry standard for cities to conduct a detailed assessment of their properties every three to five years. Dallas hasn’t done that since 2017,” we wrote. “And for years, the city hasn’t been spending enough to maintain what it owns. The 2025–2026 budget currently allocates $14 million. Based on the value of the city’s holdings (around $1.5 billion), experts recommend at least twice the amount we’ve been spending on maintenance.” At that time, it was believed it would take at least $81 million. Since then, the city has claimed it would take anywhere from $500 million to $1 billion to restore the building and modernize it. The Coalition and other advocates argue that the city is running up the numbers in a bid to make moving more attractive. The Coaltion is using the provisions of Proposition S , a charter amendment passed in November 2024 that allows residents to sue the city if they believe it is not complying with the charter, ordinances, or state law. It also required the city to waive its governmental immunity to such suits. “This is a clear-cut case of the City trying to evade its mandatory duties through bureaucratic delay,” Chris Bowers, one of the attorneys for the Coalition, said in August. “The City Code states that the HPO ‘shall’ meet, inspect, and report, and that the City ‘must’ preserve its structures against deterioration. City officials’ continued nonperformance is not just neglect—it is a breach of fiduciary duty and a direct violation of Dallas law.” The suit asks the district court to compel the city to make repairs to “properly stabilize” City Hall and properly maintain its emergency generators. The Coalition says it is also seeking a court order to extend a predesignation moratorium that would prevent the city from demolishing the building. Typically, any building that is being considered for an historical landmark status is protected from demolition. The Coalition is asking for that moratorium to be extended for the exact amount of time the city has delayed compiling its historic designation report. The city’s attorneys have likely long been anticipating the opportunity to neuter Proposition S in court. In its motion, the city says that the charter amendment “is unconstitutional,” which renders the Coalition’s claims as “facially invalid.” The Coalition’s approach to saving the building, however, is multi-pronged. Volunteers have been collecting signatures to put a charter amendment before voters in May that would codify 1500 Marilla as the seat of government for the city. Should that pass, any move to place city operations elsewhere would require another referendum. The Coalition needed 20,000 signatures of registered Dallas voters—it says it has obtained at least 26,000 and plans to turn those in on Wednesday, November 18. From there, the Dallas City Secretary’s Office will review the petition to determine whether it has enough valid signatures from registered Dallas voters. If it does, the office will send the petition to the City Council, which is required by state law to put the proposed amendment on the ballot. So far, the last City Council meeting on the calendar is December 9, which means city staff is running out of daylight to present any updates to a relocation plan before the end of the year. It’s expected that a judge will rule on the city’s motion to dismiss before the year is out. You can see the Coalition’s lawsuit here , and the city’s motion here . Follow our ongoing coverage here . items.title: Arizona REALTORS® unveils 2027 executive committee, led by President Shane Cook
items.description: Arizona REALTORS® unveils 2027 executive committee, led by President Shane Cook by Emily Marek November 17, 2026 Paul Baker, Shane Cook, M. Teresa Rubio, Gunner Mitchell and Scott Drucker (via Arizona REALTORS®) Shane Cook will lead the 2027 Arizona REALTORS® executive committee, which was revealed by the association at its annual Leadership Conference in October. Theresa Rubio and Treasurer Gunner Mitchell. Baker, an agent with Engel & Völkers Scottsdale, has 40 years of Phoenix-area real estate experience. He is the former chair of the Arizona REALTORS® Legislative and Political Affairs Committee and was named Realtor of the Year by the Scottsdale Area Association of REALTORS® in 2021. Rubio, an agent with Full House Realty of Arizona in Litchfield Park, has over 20 years of industry experience and served as 2019 president of the former West Maricopa Association of REALTORS® and Region 2 vice president for Arizona REALTORS®. I’m confident in their leadership and ability to represent our members well in the year ahead.” In addition to announcing 2027 officers at the Leadership Conference, Arizona REALTORS® also named Immediate Past President Lisa Paffrath of Better Homes and Gardens Real Estate Grand View North in Flagstaff the 2026 Arizona REALTOR® of the Year. Economy: Solid Fundamentals Bay Area nonfarm employment increased year-over-year (YOY) by 0.9% to over 4.0 million. At the same time, the unemployment rate declined by 40 basis points (bps) to 4.1%. Employment growth is expected to continue rising over the next 12 months. Median household income increased by 6.7% YOY, to $153,800, remaining the highest of all metropolitan markets in the US. While tech layoffs have persisted, the artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) sector continues to expand its hiring and concurrently leasing large blocks of space. Through the third quarter of 2026, Bay Area-based companies captured 75.9% ($324.5 billion) of venture capital funding into AI/ML in the U.S. Supply and Demand: Demand Outpaces Supply Vacancy fell across the Bay Area for the 12th consecutive quarter, to 3.9%, as new construction has not been able to keep up with increasing demand. Vacancy is down 110 bps YOY and currently sits at the lowest level since the fourth quarter of 2007. Net absorption has slowed in back-to-back quarters, as deliveries have been quiet, but remains positive, with 2,077 units absorbed in the third quarter. As the number of available units continues to dwindle, absorption may continue to slow until new supply meets demand. Units delivered in the third quarter totaled 969, up 306 units from the prior quarter but down by over 500 units YOY. Excluding the prior quarter, it was the lowest quarterly total since the second quarter of 2013. The pipeline, however, is growing, as units under construction have risen for five consecutive quarters, reaching 18,625 units through the third quarter. The National Association of Home Builders (NAHB)/ Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) fell four points to 25 in November, representing the weakest homebuilder confidence reading since April 2012. Builders have relied ever more heavily on discounts and mortgage buydown tactics to move inventory, with NAHB reporting that 46% of builders cut prices during the month, the highest share since the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic. Typical discounts ran flat at 6% for the eighth straight month, and 68% of builders used sales incentives, another post-Covid high. It was the 20th consecutive month that at least 60% of builders had featured margin-eroding price-cut promotions. Further, in November, all three of the key HMI components sank. items.title: Custom Home Building Share Rises in 2025
items.description: Custom Home Building Share Rises in 2025 November 17, 2026 Ashok Chaluvadi No Comments Custom homes accounted for 19.6 % of all single-family homes started in 2025 up from the 17.5 % in 2024. The custom home market consists of contractor-built and owner-built houses—homes built one at a time for owner occupancy on the owner’s land, with either the owner or a builder acting as a general contractor. The alternatives are homes built for sale (on the builder’s land, often in subdivisions, with the intention of selling the house and land in one transaction) and homes built for rent. In 2025, 71.8 % of the single-family homes started were built for sale, and 8.6 % were built for rent according to the most recent release of the Census Bureau’s Survey of Construction (SOC). While the custom-home percentage increased in 2025, the number of custom homes started in 2025 (182,869) also increased compared to the number of custom homes started in 2024 (176,932). Quarterly published statistics show that the custom-home share of single-family starts remained flat in 2026. Although the quarterly statistics are more timely, they lack the geographic detail available in the annual data set. When analyzed across the nine census divisions, the annual data show that the highest custom home share in 2025 was 47.0% in the New England division. items.title: Ackman says Trump can still end GSE conservatorships, relist this term
items.description: Bill Ackman still believes Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can be relisted on the New York Stock Exchange and exit their conservatorships before the end of President Donald Trump’s second term, even after Democrats won control of both chambers in the midterm elections. In a letter to Pershing Square Holdings shareholders signed in early November, Ackman, the company's founder and CEO, and chief investment officer Ryan Israel wrote that “a relisting and release from conservatorship can be accomplished by the President using his executive authority without any involvement of Congress ." They argue that the administration has a political incentive to act before 2029 to avoid “handing control” of the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) to a future administration, given the influence they have over housing policy. Ackman and Israel said the GSEs can be released “in a manner that maintains and enhances mortgage affordability while maximizing the long-term value of American taxpayers’ 79.9% ownership of the two companies.” The Department of the Treasury holds warrants to acquire 79.9% of each enterprise’s common stock. Pershing first detailed a road map in November 2025. The plan begins with a new agreement between the Treasury and the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) that addresses repayment or restructuring of Treasury’s senior preferred stock. The next step would be for the Treasury to exercise its warrants to purchase 79.9% of the GSEs' common shares. The final step would be FHFA approval for the GSEs to relist on the NYSE as privately owned operating companies. “The relisting and release of F2 will be one of the few major pieces of economic policy the President can still achieve after the midterms,” Ackman and Israel wrote. “We believe that there is no credible alternative to F2 exiting conservatorship and relisting on the NYSE as private-sector-owned operating companies.” The memo also says Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has indicated the administration will focus on the GSEs and their future ownership status in 2027 and 2028. 18 years under consevatorship Fannie and Freddie have been in conservatorship for 18 years. According to the Pershing memo, they now have more than $200 billion of shareholder equity. Over the past decade, average annual credit losses have been “only 0.05%,” and current capital levels are described as roughly 50 times that loss rate. Ackman and Israel estimate that combined capital could grow to more than $375 billion over the next five years, or more than 4% of the mortgage-backed securities guaranteed by the enterprises. On valuation, the memo says the GSEs currently trade at about 1.5 times their earnings. From Trump’s election through the end of last year, when talk of a relisting was more active, their share prices rose by about eight times. This year, by contrast, their share prices have fallen more than 60% as the administration has remained “silent” on the issue, the investors said. Pershing Square is heavily exposed to the outcome. The fund holds about 99 million shares of Fannie Mae, with a market value of roughly $422.5 million, along with roughly 95 million shares of Freddie Mac valued at about $386.9 million, according to the memo. items.title: Mortgage rates jump to 7.58% as inflation lifts bond yields
items.description: Mortgage rates skyrocketed last week on the back of rising inflation and bond yields, erasing some of the recent affordability gains for potential homebuyers. At HousingWire 's Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, rates for 30-year conforming loans averaged 7.58%, up 23 basis points from one week ago . Rates for 30-year jumbo loans jumped 31 bps to average 7.87%, while rates for 30-year loans through the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) rose 15 bps to 7.37%. HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami wrote over the weekend that "last week wasn't good for mortgage rates or the bond market" due to hawkish statements from Federal Reserve officials and hot inflation data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Additionally, the U.S. conflict with Iran and potential tariff increases against Mexico propelled long-term Treasury rates and mortgage rates upward. Interest rate traders took notice. According to the CME Group 's FedWatch tool , more than 93% expect benchmark rates to increase by 25 bps at next month's Fed meeting. That's up from 76% one month ago. It would be the second hike of the year by the Fed and put the federal funds rate at a range of 4% to 4.25%. Kyle Bass, business production manager at Refi.com , pointed to Mortgage Bankers Association application data showing that recent downward moves in rates had positive impacts on loan demand . But with visible volatility in rates on a day-to-day basis, he said, preparation between loan officers and borrowers is needed to lock in the lowest possible rate and get lower monthly payments. "Borrowers who benefit are the ones who prepared before the number moved. A shadow application, with income documents, statements and credit in order, lets a homeowner ask what their current mortgage could do for them the day rates cooperate. Waiting for a better number only works if you are ready when it arrives," Bass said. Better affordability in new homes? A report released Tuesday by Realtor.com shows that the new-home segment is giving the typical buyer lower rates and better affordability than existing homes. Homebuilders, who are also under financial pressure, continue to offer rate buydowns and other incentives as they seek to offload their inventory. Realtor.com reported that the average mortgage rate for a new-home buyer in the third quarter was 5.01%, more than a full percentage point lower than the 6.15% rate for an existing-home buyer. That translates to a difference of $258 in monthly payments for someone buying a $400,000 home with a 10% down payment . "Builders have adjusted to a market where affordability is still a major hurdle, but that adjustment isn't always visible in the listing price," Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com, said in a statement. "Reduced mortgage rates can help make a new home more affordable for buyers while allowing builders to hold asking prices relatively steady." The report noted that reduced rates are often temporary and only last for the first few years after origination. But even when comparing 30-year fixed rates, those who bought a new home in the third quarter saved, with average rates of 6.19% compared to 6.68% for existing home-buyers. On the same $400,000 purchase with 10% down, the new-home buyer saves about $117 per month in interest. "Mortgage-rate incentives can make a meaningful difference in what a buyer pays each month, but it's important to understand how long the lower rate lasts," Berner said. "A temporary buydown can provide relief early on, while a lower rate fixed for the life of the loan offers a different kind of savings." Selma Hepp , chief economist at Cotality , said in a statement that tariff-driven increases to building materials are putting pressure on the new-home segment. In turn, this winds up being felt by consumers through higher home purchase prices. Regardless of the type of home being purchased, rising insurance premiums and property taxes are also straining budgets. "For housing, the key question is not simply whether mortgage rates decline, but whether they fall enough to meaningfully improve purchasing power and bring more buyers and sellers back to the market," Hepp said." Until then, I expect activity to remain relatively subdued, making the spring homebuying season an increasingly important test of whether the market can finally turn a corner." Persistent strength in the economy While housing market professionals continue to grapple with fewer home sales and lower mortgage origination volumes, the U.S. economy as a whole continues to show resilience to inflation, tariffs and geopolitical uncertainty. Melissa Cohn, regional vice president at William Raveis Mortgage , pointed to last week's Producer Price Index (PPI), which showed 6.5% inflation on an annualized basis in October. It was the largest year-over-year increase since November 2022. That came only days after the Consumer Price Index showed monthly inflation of 0.4%. “Unfortunately, the CPI number that we got earlier this week has set off bond yields, and bond yields were probably up almost 25 basis points from where they were at the end of the previous week," Cohn said Friday in a statement. items.title: LAHSA To Return $150M Of HUD Funding In Finalized Settlement
items.description: A federal judge signed an agreement between the Department of Housing and Urban Development and the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority , removing the LA program from HUD oversight. The settlement resolves an ongoing dispute in which HUD suspended payments to LAHSA amid a fraud investigation. The agreement requires LAHSA to give back about $150M in federal funding. HUD previously announced the deal, but it is now final, the agency said in a release Tuesday . The agreement also shifts federal money from LAHSA to the Los Angeles County government in stages, LAist reported , adding that the deal preserves the LA region’s request for $240M in annual federal funding for housing services. Pixabay/ValterM Databases and systems maintained by LAHSA will switch over to the county over the coming months, and tighter oversight will be implemented. “Today's settlement closes a difficult chapter for LAHSA and allows us to move forward with greater clarity and stability,” LAHSA interim CEO Gita O’Neill said in a release. “Our focus now is on working closely with our local partners to ensure continuity of services, support an orderly transition, and remain true to our mission of connecting our unhoused neighbors with the services, resources, and pathways to housing they need.” LAHSA has been the subject of scrutiny at the local level since at least 2024, when an LA County audit found that the organization mismanaged hundreds of millions of dollars for homeless services. Executives connected with organizations that received money from LAHSA were charged with misappropriating millions of dollars, including an instance of homeless funds allegedly being diverted to a nightclub . An LAist investigation last year showed that a former LAHSA co-CEO finalized a $2.1M contract with a nonprofit where her husband was an executive, despite telling the publication she was recused from the decision-making. HUD officials, including Secretary Scott Turner, pointed the finger for the removal directly at LAHSA. “Year after year, LAHSA funneled billions of dollars in federal funding to organizations with no oversight, which resulted in nothing but skyrocketing homelessness, failing at their most basic responsibility,” Turner said in HUD’s statement. But U.S. District Judge David Carter, who presided over the case, placed blame at the feet of both LAHSA and HUD. “This has been an absolute past dereliction of duty by the federal government,” Carter said at a Friday hearing, as reported by LAist. “I termed it a partnership in failure,” he said. “Local government turned an absolute blind eye to the distribution of these funds and transparency and accountability for these funds.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register

items.title: Aging Parents and Empty Nests Force Homeowners To Rethink Layouts Years Before the Move
items.description: Most homeowners know their homes may need updates to accommodate their changing needs as they age. Some, however, are thinking even further ahead. Instead of waiting until those changes are necessary, they’re investing in renovations years in advance to prepare for aging parents who might eventually move in after their children leave the nest. Angi’s 2026 State of Home Spending Pulse study found that 66% of homeowners plan to make a major home investment within the next five years. And the 2027 Home Trends To Watch report predicts that 2027 will be the year they take a proactive approach and focus on creating a home that grows with them. If you own your home, experts agree that you should anticipate how your needs could change in the next five to 10 years and use that information to guide your long-term home improvement goals today. By doing so, you can make the most out of your renovation budget, avoid costly last-minute adjustments, and ensure your home comfortably adapts to the different stages of life. What's driving this trend? Matt Plaskoff, CEO and founder of One Week Bath in Los Angeles , is seeing this proactive, multigenerational "future-proofing” trend among his clients. “It comes down to people having heard stories of it going the other way. Mom falls or receives a diagnosis, and suddenly the family is trying to put in a walk-in shower and grab bars on short notice while suddenly incurring more costs with doctors and insurance,” says Plaskoff. Multigenerational living is also at an all-time high, and the recent National Association of Realtors® Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers report reflects this shift. It found that 17% of homes purchased last year were intended for multigenerational households. And when adult kids leave, there’s suddenly more space that makes it easier to create a home that works well for both aging in place and aging parents. We can’t forget the housing affordability crisis forcing families to rethink the homes they already own. “The house may no longer fit the household, but buying a better-fitting home can mean a higher price, a higher mortgage rate, and higher monthly expenses,” says Jon Brooks , co-founder of Momentum Realty in Jacksonville, FL . Plus, it's more cost-effective to future-proof your home when you plan properly and actually have the funds to support your projects. “The worst time to remodel is when you don’t have the budget for it. You make decisions that should take time and careful planning under pressure and may just accept whatever contractor can show up ASAP, even if it means you have to pay more,” says Plaskoff. There is also a practical side. If you're already opening up walls for a bath remodel, for example, adding blocking for future grab bars, widening a doorway, or adding a curbless shower will be faster and cheaper than if you were to come back later and redo finished work. Loading... If you're thinking about starting a new remodeling project, think ahead to your needs. Realtor.com/Getty Images Balancing safety, privacy, and resale Experts agree that a strong universal design features a functional yet beautiful bathroom with a wider doorway, good lighting, lever handles for knobs, a walk-in shower, and slip-resistant flooring. “If done right, it feels more like a spa than a hospital, and that’s what matters most to those who are using it every day,” Plaskoff explains. A home that supports privacy and independence is just as important. “An example can be a primary suite on the ground floor with its own bathroom, or a room with a separate entrance. Parents want to keep their routines and privacy, without having to sacrifice accessibility,” says Plaskoff. You might also consider adding a second structure to your backyard like an accessory dwelling unit or tiny home. “For families with the space, an ADU is one of the best solutions we see. It gives an aging parent true independence, with their own kitchen, bath, and front door, while keeping them close enough for daily connection and support,” explains Michelle Squire , designer and principal at Studio SQUARE in San Francisco . If long-term resale is important to you, be sure to consider what buyers value in your neighborhood. This way you can determine where to make permanent changes and where to keep things flexible. “If you’re overimproving for the area, just understand you may have a harder time recouping that money if you choose to sell,” says Christina Rordam , real estate agent at Florida Realty Investments in Orlando, FL . At the end of the day, prioritize flexibility, try not to over improve for the neighborhood you’re in, and most importantly, consider what works best for you and your family.

items.title: Service Properties Trust passes on $2B all-cash offer
items.description: Service Properties Trust’s response to TKO’s unsolicited $2 billion offer for nearly 100 of the real estate investment’s assets? Thanks, but no thanks. The RMR Group-managed REIT rejected last month’s proposal by Jim Koehler’s firm, Bisnow reported . The investment firm was seeking to acquire all 77 hotels left in the real estate investment trust’s hospitality portfolio and 93 properties overall, but the board was unanimous in its rejection. An activist investor, Blackwells Capital, pushed back against the rejection before it was made public, claiming there was a conflict of interest around RMR and hotel operator Sonesta International Hotels around termination and transition fees. But the board was unmoved, writing to Blackwells that it “believes that allowing this growth to take hold before selling offers the opportunity to realize significantly higher proceeds for shareholders than selling the hotels today,” citing a belief the hotels could be worth between $3 billion and $4.1 billion in the aggregate. TKO’s substantial offer immediately raised red flags among analysts. For starters, the offer was more than double the market capitalization of the entire company, which is less than $1 billion; the hotels only make up a sliver of the company asset portfolio. SIGN UP Additionally, there’s little record online of TKO and scant evidence the firm can execute a deal of such significant size. TKO offered to deposit $50 million in an escrow fund a week after its initial proposal The offer came at an inflection point for the REIT, which trades under SVC on the Nasdaq and is pivoting to a net-lease-focused entity. It had sold 66 hotels for $534 million in December, bringing its hotel sales for the year to 112 properties and nearly 15,000 rooms for a collective $859 million. The REIT is working to improve its balance sheet and manage approximately $5.8 billion in debt maturities coming over the next five years. It plans to sell off its hotels itself in the coming years. SVC posted a net loss of $87.9 million in the third quarter, an increase from the $46.9 million lost during the same period last year. Its stock has jumped up in recent days, though it’s down nearly 30 percent in the last year. — Holden Walter-Warner Read more Commercial National Unsolicited $2B cash bid for 93-hotel collection raises red flags

items.title: A Short List of Very Good Thanksgiving Shortcuts in Dallas
items.description: Live Poll How does this post find you? Feeling confident about the holidays? Gift lists already crossed off? New York Times holiday recipes tested and ready for the big show? Or does this post find you stressed? Anxiously wringing a kitchen hand towel as you mull over the contents of your pantry and envision a harrowing journey to Central Market? If it’s the latter, stop that! This year has already been much too long, and the last thing you need right now is to worry about making fancy food. Let somebody else do that. Below, I’m making a handful of Dallas Thanksgiving to-go recommendations from places that would never and could never let you down. Because the second-to-last thing you need right now is a lengthy listicle. Zavala’s BBQ One of two recommendations from our Best BBQ list , Zavala’s is vacuum-sealing whole briskets ($225) and whole turkey breasts ($75) with reheating instructions that will make you look like a pro. Pick it up at Mas Coffee Co., just down the road from Zavala’s charming, high-energy restaurant in Grand Prairie. $75 for a whole turkey breast; $225 for a whole brisket. Order by Nov. 23. Pickup on Nov. 25 at Mas Coffee Co. More details Walkers’ Bar & Market It would be a bit much to hire a sommelier for your Thanksgiving dinner. But picking up a selection of wines picked by Walkers’ Bar & Market co-owner and advanced sommelier-certified Rosemary Walker-Green is totally within play. $125 for a three-wine bundle. Order by Nov. 20. Pickup by Nov. 24–25, noon–2 p.m., at Walkers’ Bar & Market. More details . Bresnan Bread and Pastry If the photos of Bresnan’s black bottom pecan pies, Parker House rolls, cinnamon rolls , or spiced pumpkin tea cakes aren’t enough to inspire your Thanksgiving pre-order, you’re either allergic to gluten or something quite dire is afoot. Pies $32–$44; Parker House rolls $25. Order by Nov. 20 at 3 p.m. Pickup on Nov. 24 – 25, 8 a.m.–2 p.m., at the McKinney bakery, or Nov. 25, 8 – 11 a.m., at Saint Michael and All Angels Episcopal Church in Dallas. More details . Café Momentum For a feel-good meal that feeds your family and provides life-changing mentorship, the young and award-winning chefs at Café Momentum are packing up scratch-made gravy, brioche rolls, collard greens, mashed potatoes, cider-brined turkey, and more—all ready to reheat for a family of four. $195. Order by Nov. 20. Pickup on Nov. 25 at Cafe Momentum. More details . Georgie In addition to a whole 12-pound turkey, the Travis Street restaurant ( newly reinstated on our 50 Best Restaurants guide) is packing up duckfat cornbread pudding, cranberry marmalade, brown butter sweet potato puree, kuri squash soup, and optional caviar add-ons for a refined family feast. From $325. Order by Nov. 21. More details . Hurtado In the spirit of this spot’s massive menu, the second recommendation from our Best BBQ list is offering a wide range of Thanksgiving options. Choose from a whole holiday brisket, rack of beef ribs, glazed holiday ham, or poblano and pepper jack sausage paired with sides like hatch mac and cheese, brisket beans, stuffing, and street corn. À la carte meats from $39.49; whole briskets $175. Order by Nov. 19. Pickup on Nov. 25 by 6 p.m. at your selected Hurtado location. More details . Meridian Our dining critic Brian Reinhart called the Sunday night fried chicken dinner at the recently revamped Meridian some of the best he’s ever tasted . I’m inclined to trust him! And maybe inclined to splurge on a whole bird, along with pimento grits, cornbread, broccolini, and burnt honey tart pie for spicy at-home Thanksgiving. A portion of the proceeds will be donated to Meat Fight . $125 for four or $225 for eight. Order by Nov. 23, while supplies last. Pickup on Nov. 25, 10 a.m. – 3 p.m., at Meridian. More details Kuby's Sausage House A few years ago, we decided to host Thanksgiving right after moving into a new house. I don't recommend doing that. But I do recommend ordering your turkey (or beef tenderloin, or prime rib) from Kuby's , a Snider Plaza institution for a reason. My family may have had to fight over chairs that Thanksgiving, but our bird was perfection. $125 for a smoked turkey platter serving 12–15. Call 214-363-2231 to order and confirm the Thanksgiving deadline and pickup details. More details . items.title: Congress eyes overhaul that could pile billions in fees on data center developers
items.description: The data centers pacing the AI boom could get a faster path to power, but at a steep price. A sweeping congressional permitting proposal would make it easier to build data center infrastructure, while potentially saddling developers with billions of dollars in additional electricity costs, the New York Times reported . The bill would streamline federal environmental reviews for projects including transmission lines, gas pipelines and power generation facilities, potentially easing one of the biggest obstacles to data center development: securing enough electricity to operate. But it would also force data centers to pay more to access the electric grid, shifting costs historically spread among utility customers. One provision would direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to establish rules requiring data centers to cover both the cost of grid upgrades needed to serve them and the expense of using existing transmission infrastructure. The proposal would upend longstanding regulatory principles that prevent utilities from charging customers twice for the same grid capacity. Federal grid charges alone could cost data centers an additional $35 billion over the next decade, according to a report from consulting firm Grid Strategies. States could potentially collect another $136 billion under separate provisions. “The day of data center freeloading ends when this bill passes,” said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a co-author of the bill. The Data Center Coalition, a prominent trade group, has not taken a stance yet on the bill. SIGN UP The proposal arrives as data center developers face mounting political resistance over the facilities’ enormous power demands. Many campuses consume as much electricity as small cities, raising concerns about infrastructure costs, utility bills and the strain on local grids. Voters approved at least 40 local ballot initiatives restricting data centers in this month’s midterm elections. For developers, the legislation presents a complicated trade-off. Faster federal approvals could help unlock power infrastructure and make more sites viable. But higher electricity costs could alter project economics, particularly in markets where grid capacity is already constrained. The bill could also encourage data center development on federal land, where the Interior Department is considering at least 17 applications, according to the Center for Western Priorities. Even if Congress moves forward, state and local approvals would remain a hurdle. — Holden Walter-Warner Read more Development Texas Love ‘em or hate ‘em, data centers grab real estate spotlight in Texas elections
