items.title: Why Women’s Financial Wellness Is About More Than Money
items.description: Live Poll What does it mean to be financially well? For some, it might mean having enough saved for retirement. For others, it's knowing their children will be taken care of, having the freedom to pursue a new opportunity, or simply feeling confident about the future. But financial wellness rarely exists on its own. The decisions women make about money are often closely connected to their families, careers, personal well-being, and the lives they want to build. That connection was at the heart of a recent Dallas gathering, "A Life Well Lived Is Thoughtfully Curated," hosted by Bernstein Private Wealth Management , where women came together to explore what it means to live well--and why wealth is only one part of the equation. Women are becoming an increasingly powerful financial force Research has long been at the center of Bernstein, and within that, it's become increasingly clear that more and more women are stepping into wealth--and that women often view and manage wealth in a different way than men. "There's a huge wealth transfer that's imminent, and women are at the helm of that," explained wealth advisor Julie Judson , one of the event's hosts. "Women are going to inherit wealth from their parents and from their spouses over the next several decades, and we still believe that women are under-resourced." "They're not spoken to the way that men are in the rooms that we are in in our industry," Judson added. "We have the opportunity here in Dallas to influence how female investors are spoken to, how they're educated, and how they're empowered, and that's something we really want to do." Event hosts Julie Judson and Cecily Bolding were joined by nine panelists that led three sessions that highlight women's wellness in the home, wellness within, and financial wellness. (Photo provided by Bernstein Private Wealth Management) Why financial wellness and personal wellness go hand in hand As more women step into these positions, Bernstein is finding that the idea of financial success can look very different for those women. "What we notice from female investors is there's a theme of longevity. 'I want to make sure this provides longevity for me and my stakeholders, whether it's charity or family,'" explained Cecily Bolding , managing director at Bernstein and event co-host. "Understanding what women want out of investments and out of wellness, it's inextricably linked." That was the inspiration behind the event for Bernstein, which highlighted common areas of stress for women: wellness in the home, wellness within, and wellness with wealth. items.title: ARMLS named among defendants in new Compass litigation
items.description: ARMLS named among defendants in new Compass litigation by Emily Marek November 16, 2026 ARMLS is one of 15 MLSs named in a new slate of Compass lawsuits. Compass filed new antitrust lawsuits against 15 different MLSs, with the Arizona Regional Multiple Listing Service named among the defendants. All MLSs named in Compass’ new slate of suits have rules that require real estate agents to share listings with the MLS when they begin publicly marketing those properties, a practice that directly contradicts Compass’ highly contested three-phase marketing strategy . “Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass representative said in a press release. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.” In its complaint against ARMLS, Compass called the group a “competition-killing real estate industry organization” and asserted that ARMLS and its “co-conspirators” have banded together to “deprive homeowners of choice.” In addition to ARMLS, the listing services named in Compass lawsuits include: bridgeMLS Bay East MLS Canopy MLS Contra Costa MLS Doorify MLS Houston Association of REALTORS® Hive MLS MLSListings The MLS-CLAW NorthstarMLS OneKey MLS REcolorado San Diego MLS Stellar MLS ARMLS previously was one of seven plaintiffs — all named in Compass’ suit — to file a joint complaint against Compass in October. In the complaint, the MLSs alleged that Compass policies give the brokerage an unfair market advantage by withholding properties from the general public. Compass, meanwhile, maintains that its lawsuits will ultimately decide whether homeowners or MLSs get to decide how properties are marketed. “It’s almost as if these MLSs are asking people to ignore the evidence that proves their claims aren’t true,” the Compass representative added. “For years, seven of the top 25 MLSs, covering 340,000 agents across 12 states, have allowed agents to publicly market ‘office exclusives’ without fines, and none of the problems they warn about have happened. If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30% of the country?” ARMLS did not respond to Phoenix Agent’s request for comment by the time of publication. items.title: Hot Property: A Dallas Midcentury Modern With Richardson Zoning
items.description: Live Poll Built in 1966, 13321 Purple Sage Road is a midcentury modern home that makes the most of its relationship with the outdoors. Set beneath a canopy of mature magnolia and maple trees in North Dallas' coveted, the residence pairs natural textures with floor-to-ceiling windows that draw in the surrounding greenery. The design balances the simplicity of midcentury architecture with a variety of materials, from hardwood floors to natural stone and tile. The result feels connected to its 1960s era without being overly nostalgic, with a serene and understated aesthetic. We first brought you this home nearly two years ago, when it last changed hands. Since then, the current owners have invested heavily in new HVAC, plumbing, and electrical systems; added a whole-home generator (increasingly handy given Texas' unpredictable weather); and made aesthetic updates throughout. The house is better for all of them. Its location in a MCM-laden enclave of Far North Dallas—which feeds into Richardson schools and is within minutes of the planned new Dallas Mavericks arena—is a not-so-small bonus. Walking into the home, the sunken living room makes an immediate impression with a substantial brick fireplace anchoring the space. Expansive windows stretch across the back of the home, framing views of the backyard beyond. Stone and tile flooring introduce a variety of textures and tones, contrasting with the golden hues of the hardwood floors found elsewhere. In the kitchen, wood cabinetry brings a welcome dose of warmth to the home’s restrained palette. Its rich finish stands out against the neutral backsplash, giving the space a classic midcentury feel. Elsewhere, shades of green appear throughout the interiors, from the home office to the primary bedroom. The bathrooms continue the home’s appreciation for natural materials, with one standout featuring a sink carved from natural stone. Its organic shape complements the wooden vanity, the earth-toned tiled shower, and the terrazzo tile floors. Outside, the backyard unfolds as a landscape of winding pathways, mature trees, and carefully considered seating areas. Rather than one broad, flat expanse of lawn, the design takes advantage of the sloped grounds as curved paths lead to different sections of the garden. A heated pool and surrounding pool deck offer elevated views of the landscape beyond, while two separate seating areas provide ample room for hosting outdoors. This midcentury residence understands the appeal of its surroundings and perfectly fits within the landscape, rather than trying to work against it. The home allows nature to inspire its design and its original era to take the lead. See more of this house .
